candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9999 malware probability, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, with SHAP values from +0.006300 to +0.016850. However, the evidence is weak for a cryptojacking-specific call. Every n-gram has a reported relative frequency of 0.000000, and no function locations are listed, so none of these patterns can be tied to a specific routine. Almost all of the n-grams are generic compiler-generated instruction pairs: stack and call setup (PUSH SUB, CALL ADD, ADD POP, LEA CALL, SUB LEA, MOV LEA), flag-test branches (TEST JZ, TEST JS, MOV JZ, CMP JL) and conditional moves (CMOVZ MOV, CMP CMOVZ, XOR CMOVNZ). The XOR-heavy and shift patterns (XOR XOR, XOR SHL, XOR MOV, XOR CALL, CALL XOR) are loosely compatible with hash or bit-mixing code of the kind found in mining algorithms. They are also common in ordinary code such as register zeroing and arithmetic, so on their own they do not show a mining routine. The evidence includes no API names, strings, constants or function-level context. The model's malware signal looks real, but this evidence cannot confirm that it is cryptojacking specifically. The case is therefore inconclusive and needs further analysis.
